up.note: Theorem 16 of [BdW02]: the algorithm must spend $\ge 1/3$ expected queries in each sensitive block. Nisan's argument only ever compares the algorithm's behaviour on $x$ and on $x^{B_i}$, and both of those are in $\mathrm{Dom}(f)$ by the definition of a sensitive block, so it never uses totality. Concretely: if the algorithm touched $B_i$ with probability $<1/3$ on $x$, its output distributions on $x$ and $x^{B_i}$ would be too close for it to be correct on both.

up.note: Ambainis'' basic bound applied to a single maximally block-sensitive input. Take $x$ attaining $\mathrm{bs}(f)=b$ with disjoint sensitive blocks $B_1,\dots,B_b$, and let $R$ relate $x$ to the $b$ inputs $x^{B_j}$. Then $m_x = b$, $m_y = 1$, and because the blocks are disjoint each index $i$ lies in at most one of them, so $\ell_x=\ell_y=1$. The bound $\sqrt{m_x m_y/(\ell_x \ell_y)}$ is $\sqrt b$. Nothing here needs $f$ total: each $x^{B_j}$ is a domain point by the definition of a sensitive block.

    $\mathrm{Adv}(\vee_n)=\sqrt n$, which the barrier above also caps at $\sqrt{\mathrm{C}^0\mathrm{C}^1}=\sqrt n$. The exponent $2$ is optimal and the cell closes.

The two-sided refinement $\mathrm{Adv}(f) = \Omega\big(\sqrt{\mathrm{bs}^{0}(f)\, \mathrm{bs}^{1}(f)}\big)$ comes out of the same relation with $X$ and $Y$ both taken to be large, and is what pins $\mathrm{Adv}$ on functions like \(\mathrm{ADDR}_k\); it is not a two-measure statement, so it lives in the notes rather than in the matrix. Composed with $\mathrm{s}\le\mathrm{bs}$ this record also supplies $\mathrm{s}\le\mathrm{Adv}^2$, and with $\mathrm{Adv}\le\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm}=\Theta(\mathrm{Q})$ it recovers the classic $\mathrm{Q}=\Omega(\sqrt{\mathrm{bs}})$.
